extracted.intended_audience: mathematics teachers and instructors (those teaching problem-solving)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for instructors on how to lead students through problem-solving: understanding the problem, devising a plan, carrying out the plan, and looking back, with recommended questioning techniques and checks. Emphasizes heuristics, classroom dialogue, and how to give unobtrusive hints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four phases of problem solving
rubrics_metrics.description: First, understand the problem; second, see how the items are connected to obtain the idea of the solution (make a plan); third, carry out the plan; fourth, look back at the completed solution, review and discuss it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shift viewpoint repeatedly as you work; do not omit any phase — omitting a phase (especially understanding) leads to mistakes. The teacher should prompt students through these phases by questions and suggestions and help them acquire the habit of following them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the problem (identify unknown/data/condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The verbal statement must be understood; the student should be able to state the problem fluently and point out the principal parts: the unknown, the data, the condition. (Questions: 'What is the unknown? What are the data? What is the condition?')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teacher can check understanding by asking students to repeat the statement and identify parts. The problem should also be natural and interesting; allow time for presentation. Understanding includes a desire for the solution and considering whether the condition is satisfiable (provisional guess).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use figures and suitable notation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a figure is connected with the problem the student should draw it and indicate on it the unknown and the data; introduce suitable notation and choose appropriate signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Devoting attention to choice of signs obliges the student to consider the objects involved. Drawing and notation help clarify parts of the problem and make subsequent reasoning easier (illustrated repeatedly in the parallelepiped/diagonal example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask if the condition is possible (provisional check)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the preparatory stage the student should consider whether it is possible to satisfy the condition (a provisional answer or guess is acceptable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This question prevents wasted effort on impossible or ill-posed problems and helps the student form initial intuition; it need not be a definitive answer but a reasonable check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devise a plan by relating to prior problems and knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: To get a plan, recall related problems, formerly solved problems, or theorems; look at the unknown and try to think of a familiar problem having the same or a similar unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good ideas are based on past experience and knowledge. Use the contact point of the unknown to find analogous solved problems. The text recommends the explicit question: 'Do you know a related problem?' and exploiting any such relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary, transform or modify the problem to find a route
rubrics_metrics.description: If known related problems do not help, vary the problem (generalize, specialize, use analogy, drop part of the condition) to find an auxiliary or related problem that is solvable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variation may lead to an auxiliary problem whose solution can be used. But beware of straying too far — use the returning question 'Did you use all the data? Did you use the whole condition?' to come back to the original problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use auxiliary problems or introduce auxiliary elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce an auxiliary problem or element (e.g., an auxiliary line/triangle) whose unknown can be computed and used to eliminate auxiliaries and obtain the desired unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The classroom example introduces a right triangle as an auxiliary element to reduce the parallelepiped diagonal to Pythagorean steps. Teacher may prompt progressively until students introduce the decisive auxiliary element themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: When trying approaches, prefer looking at the unknown
rubrics_metrics.description: When many related problems exist, choose those problems that share a common point — look at the unknown and try to think of a familiar problem having the same or a similar unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This heuristic narrows the search to useful analogies; it is explicitly recommended as a way to pick among many somewhat-related problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use all the data / check that no data are ignored
rubrics_metrics.description: Always check whether all given data have been used: 'Did you use all the data? Did you use the whole condition?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to use all data or ignoring parts of the condition is a common source of errors or incomplete solutions. This question helps keep the work anchored to the original problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carry out the plan patiently and check each step
rubrics_metrics.description: The plan gives an outline; carrying it out requires patience and checking each step one after the other until everything is perfectly clear and no obscure corner remains where an error could be hidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the student conceived the plan themselves they are less likely to forget it; if they accepted it by authority they may forget. The teacher should insist that the student checks each step; pick out 'touchy' points for rechecking in long or involved arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require honest conviction of correctness (insight vs formal proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should be honestly convinced of the correctness of each step, either 'intuitively' (seeing) or 'formally' (proving).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teacher may emphasize the difference between seeing and proving: 'Can you see clearly that the step is correct? But can you also prove that the step is correct?' Use discretion in pressing for formal proofs depending on students' background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Looking back: review, reexamine, and try to improve solution
rubrics_metrics.description: After obtaining and writing the solution the student should 'look back' — reconsider and reexamine the result and the path that led to it to consolidate knowledge and develop problem-solving ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage verifications, alternate derivations, and searching for improvements or other applications. Students often miss this phase; teachers should impress its importance and lead students through questions like 'Can you check the result?' and 'Can you check the argument?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify results by multiple tests and alternative derivations
rubrics_metrics.description: Test the result by different means: obtain the result differently, check special/limiting cases, use symmetry, dimensional analysis, monotonicity, proportionality, or other intuitive tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example tests: do all data appear in the formula? Is the formula symmetric in a,b,c? If c→0 does the result reduce to the plane case? Does unit scaling behave correctly? These 'experimental' checks increase confidence and aid memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer learning: ask whether result or method applies elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage students to imagine cases where the result or the method could be utilized again: 'Can you use the result, or the method, for some other problem?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide or encourage concrete applications (e.g., the cafeteria or flagpole cable problems) and exploration of related configurations; this consolidates understanding and shows connections between problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher's method of questioning: general-to-specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with a general question or suggestion and, if necessary, come down gradually to more specific and concrete questions or suggestions until one elicits a response; repeat from a general question when helping exploit a student's idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with simple, natural and general suggestions; come down gradually to maximise the student's share of the work. Be prepared to use a gamut of progressively more explicit hints if needed. Study examples carefully and trial the method cautiously in class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep suggestions simple, natural, general and short
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestions must be simple and natural (so they stay unobtrusive), general (applicable to many problems to develop ability), and the list of suggestions should be short.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A short, simple, general list can be often and naturally repeated so that students assimilate the questions and develop mental habits; overly elaborate lists are less likely to be assimilated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rigid, mechanical procedures; maintain elasticity
rubrics_metrics.description: The method must not be rigid or pedantic; it should admit elasticity, variation, and different approaches so that questions asked by the teacher could plausibly have occurred to the student.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow different approaches (e.g., analogies, representing 3D as 2D) and adapt the questioning to the students' responses; the goal is to provoke thinking, not to force a single script.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good vs. bad questions: avoid telling the method outright
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overly specific hints that give the whole secret away or are meaningful only to students already near the solution (example of a bad question: 'Could you apply the theorem of Pythagoras?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such specific suggestions may fail those who need help most, give away the solution, are too special (not instructive for future problems), and do not help students learn how to find such ideas themselves. Prefer general prompts that guide toward thinking rather than answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experimentation and partial-condition strategies in constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a construction is hard, try to satisfy part of the condition first, draw figures, vary parameters, and experimentally look for loci or patterns (e.g., locus of the fourth corner of a square).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dropping part of the condition and drawing several cases (small/large squares) can lead students to conjecture the correct auxiliary construction (e.g., that the locus is a straight line). This experimental approach helps students discover the idea themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guide inquiry by repeating and rephrasing questions when silence occurs
rubrics_metrics.description: If students are silent or not responding, the teacher should be prepared to resume dialogue, repeat questions with modification, and move gradually from general to more explicit hints until a response appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers should be ready for disconcerting silence and to persist with modified prompts; they must balance giving hints and preserving student initiative. The example classroom dialogues show incremental prompting from 'Do you know a related problem?' to more concrete hints leading to the auxiliary element.
